_comment: Domain list sources for DNS Load Forge. Data-driven so a dead or retired list is a one-line edit instead of a code change. 'format' selects the parser: hosts (0.0.0.0/127.0.0.1 domain), plain (one domain per line, may include ABP ||domain^ lines), rank_csv (popularity list, e.g. 'rank,domain'; a header row is detected). 'tier' is documentation for operators: primary lists are the ones the default mixture leans on, secondary lists add volume. 'ranked' marks a list whose order encodes popularity, which drives sampling weights and which end of the list survives --max-per-category. Verified reachable 2026-10-12.
_why_blocklistproject: A domain is only ever one category, so when two sources disagree the highest-precedence category wins and the other loses the domain. That makes SUPERSET lists actively harmful here: StevenBlack's 'alternates/*' files are the base list plus extensions, so using one for adult content silently reclassified every ad domain (72,526 of them) as adult and emptied block_ads entirely. The Block List Project publishes single-topic lists, so each category stays its own.

sources.description: Block List Project: advertising domains, single-topic. The bulk of what a filter should block and what users notice least when it does.

StevenBlack unified hosts (ads + malware + tracking). The single most widely deployed host blocklist; a filter appliance must at least match it. Its malware and phishing entries are reclassified into those categories during overlap resolution.
abuse.ch URLhaus malware distribution hosts. Fresh, high-confidence, and changes daily -- the best signal that the appliance is actually pulling threat intelligence.
Block List Project malware domains. Large; supplies volume behind the URLhaus head so a filter can be judged on recall, not just on today's headlines.
Phishing Army extended blocklist. Phishing domains are short-lived, so this doubles as a test of feed freshness.
Block List Project scam domains. Small, but these are the names real users click, so they belong in the phishing group.
Block List Project adult content, single-topic. Content policy is usually enforced separately from security policy, so it is measured separately.

Block List Project tracking domains. These are the deliberate grey zone: blocking them is a policy choice, and over-blocking the CDNs and analytics that legitimate sites depend on is how a filter breaks a web application. Reported, never scored as a failure.
Cisco Umbrella top 1M. Rank order is the popularity signal that makes the traffic mix look like a real office instead of a uniform blender.
Tranco top 1M (research-oriented, aggregates several popularity sources, less commercial bias than Umbrella alone).
Majestic Million. Used for the long tail of legitimate domains, which is where a filter with an over-broad pattern can cause surprising false positives.
